title: Corporate Cognitive Warfare Expanded Edition: William Aaron Turner Releases 15,000-Word Paper on Competing for Perception Lawfully
summary: Infinitum Corporation releases the expanded edition of Corporate Cognitive Warfare, the discipline coined by William Aaron Turner, now free on Academia.edu and Zenodo.
body:
WASHINGTON, DC, November 2, 2026 - Infinitum Corporation today announced the expanded edition of "Corporate Cognitive Warfare: Irregular Warfare for Market Supremacy," a free white paper by William Aaron Turner, Founder & President of Infinitum Corporation, who coined the term Corporate Cognitive Warfare.

The expanded edition grows the original paper to about 15,000 words across 38 pages. It keeps the original definitions and the six-phase framework of Understand, Shape, Seed, Amplify, Exploit and Protect, and adds four new bodies of material for executives, communicators and security leaders.

First, a neutral doctrinal foundation. The paper reviews published research on Russian reflexive control theory, Chinese cognitive domain operations and the "three warfares," and NATO's work on cognitive warfare, drawing on sources from the Foreign Military Studies Office, the Naval Postgraduate School, RAND, the China Aerospace Studies Institute and the U.S. Department of Defense. Each tradition is presented analytically, with the caveats its own analysts raise.

Second, detailed corporate applications. Guerrilla marketing, ethical persuasion psychology, algorithmic optimization, social influence and targeted advertising are each placed inside the rules that govern them, including FTC endorsement rules, GDPR, the EU Digital Services Act, CCPA/CPRA and platform policies.

Third, twelve illustrative use cases, ranging from a challenger brand reframing its category to countering a viral falsehood, defending against a fake-review attack, responding to an executive deepfake and staying visible in AI-generated answers.

Fourth, a defensive playbook: a threat taxonomy, the DISARM shared vocabulary, narrative sensing, prebunking, decision hygiene against provocation, response tiers and regular exercises.

The paper draws a firm line. Fake accounts, bot networks, astroturfing, fabricated reviews and disinformation are treated only as threats to detect and defeat, never as tools.

The white paper is published under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license with the DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23838097.

One principle runs through all of it: win with truth, disclosure and better arguments." said William Aaron Turner, Founder & President of Infinitum Corporation.

title: Dead Reckoning Whitepaper: William Aaron Turner Gives Security Teams a Quarterly Check to Keep AI Tools Honest
summary: Infinitum Corporation's Dead Reckoning whitepaper offers security operations teams a 90-day AI adoption plan, a 12-month roadmap and a recurring quarterly verification check.
body:
WASHINGTON, DC, November 2, 2026 - Infinitum Corporation is highlighting a practical tool from its first whitepaper, "Dead Reckoning: AI for Security Operations in a Jammed, Spoofed, Watched World": a recurring quarterly check that lets security teams confirm their AI tools are still pointed in the right direction.

The paper, written by William Aaron Turner, Founder & President of Infinitum Corporation, borrows its method from navigation. When satellite signals fail, navigators fix their position from what they can verify: last known position, heading, speed, time and a second source. Turner argues that security operations centers adopting artificial intelligence need the same discipline, because a confident AI output is not the same as a correct one.

The paper sets out a sequence in three stages. A 90-day plan covers governance, a measured baseline and a pilot with analysts kept in the loop. A 12-month roadmap extends the tools that prove themselves. The quarterly dead reckoning check then compares results against the baseline and against an independent source for every critical signal.

The case for discipline rests on public data. Citing Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, the paper notes that exploiting vulnerabilities is now the top way into a breach, at 31 percent, up from 20 percent. IBM and the Ponemon Institute report that the mean time to identify and contain a breach rose to 247 days. IBM also found that organizations using security AI and automation extensively averaged USD 4.00 million per breach, against USD 5.93 million for those using none. Turner stresses that this is an association, not a guarantee.

The paper is written for security leaders, analysts and risk owners who must judge AI tools on evidence rather than vendor claims. It compares the defender's environment to one of jammed and spoofed signals and constant observation, and states plainly that this is a comparison, not a claim that any network is a front line.

Infinitum Corporation offers the paper free of charge, and readers are encouraged to check each figure against its cited source.

The paper, by William Aaron Turner, Founder & President of Infinitum Corporation, is built around one gap. In April 2022 the IMF projected that Russia's economy would shrink 8.5 percent that year. It notes, citing Castellum.AI, that Russia has faced more than twice as many sanctions designations as Iran, Syria and North Korea combined. It sets out IMF figures for 2025 showing public debt at 16.6 percent of GDP and unemployment at 2.2 percent.

The paper is presented as the author's argued position, and it gives the other side a full chapter. That chapter addresses inflation, a 14 percent key rate, growth slowing to 1.0 percent, the military burden, demographics and corruption perception, so readers can weigh both cases on the same evidence.

title: Trenches and Drones: William Aaron Turner's Second Whitepaper Treats Network Defense as a War of Attrition
summary: Infinitum Corporation releases Whitepaper No. 2, Trenches and Drones, a free guide for mid-size organizations defending networks against persistent, automated, low-cost pressure.
body:
WASHINGTON, DC, November 2, 2026 - Infinitum Corporation today released "Trenches and Drones: Network Defense for a War of Attrition," the second paper in its free whitepaper series, written by William Aaron Turner, Founder & President.

The paper starts from a plain observation: defending a network is not one big battle but a long grind of small, cheap and constant pressure. Scans that never stop, phishing waves that arrive in bursts, short floods of junk traffic and edge devices left waiting weeks for a patch all wear a defender down. Turner argues that the side that can absorb losses, repair, adapt and keep operating is the side that outlasts the other.

To make that practical, the paper reads network defense through the picture public analysts paint of the modern battlefield, which Turner summarizes as trench-style grind fused with science fiction. It walks through five fronts and pairs each battlefield feature with its equivalent on a corporate network: depth, through segmentation and identity checks at every line, with the implicit trust zone kept as small as possible as NIST SP 800-207 recommends; cheap mass, through automation that keeps the cost of defense below the cost of attack; electronic warfare, through resilience against spoofed and degraded signals; sensors, through logging and detection; and supply lines, through software and vendor risk.

The paper is written for mid-size organizations. It closes with seven recommended moves, a 30/60/90-day plan, a 12-month roadmap, a 30-item self-assessment and a scorecard, and it includes three clearly labeled hypothetical scenarios.

Turner is explicit about the limits of the comparison. The paper draws general lessons about technology and conflict from public sources such as CSIS, takes no side, makes no claim about any party and leaves out casualty, loss and performance figures for every side. "Nobody is shooting at your servers," the paper says.

Trenches and Drones follows Whitepaper No. 1, "Dead Reckoning: AI for Security Operations." Turner coined the term Corporate Cognitive Warfare, the discipline of competing for perception lawfully and defending against narrative attacks.

title: Corporate Cognitive Warfare: A Doctrine Introduction, William Aaron Turner Explains Why Markets Are Now Cognitive Battlespaces
summary: William Aaron Turner, who coined Corporate Cognitive Warfare, publishes a short doctrine introduction for executives ahead of the expanded white paper.
body:
WASHINGTON, DC, November 2, 2026 - Infinitum Corporation is highlighting "Corporate Cognitive Warfare: A Doctrine Introduction," a short, free essay by William Aaron Turner, Founder & President, who coined the term Corporate Cognitive Warfare (CCW).

The introduction opens with a warning for executives: a company's next competitor may never touch its price. Instead, it may shape what the market notices, remembers and believes, long before a buyer opens a spreadsheet. Turner argues that this contest is already under way and that most companies are fighting it without a doctrine.

The essay defines Corporate Cognitive Warfare as the disciplined application of irregular-warfare thinking to the corporate competitive environment. It treats the minds of customers, employees, investors, partners and regulators as the ground where competition is actually decided. Where conventional marketing asks how to promote a product, CCW asks how a market perceives reality, where its attention goes, how its decisions are made, and how a company earns its place in that process honestly.

The introduction sets out four core messages. Markets are now cognitive battlespaces, where attention and perception decide outcomes before price does. Military doctrine holds lessons for business when it is studied neutrally. Those lessons must be applied lawfully, inside advertising, privacy and platform rules. And every offensive capability has a defensive twin, so a company must also be able to detect and answer narrative attacks against it.

The essay is clear that CCW is not a new word for advertising and that deception is out of bounds. Fake accounts, bot networks, astroturfing and fabricated reviews are treated as threats to detect and defeat, never as tools.

The doctrine introduction serves as the entry point to the 15,000-word "Corporate Cognitive Warfare: Irregular Warfare for Market Supremacy (Expanded Edition)," which is free on Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23838097) and Academia.edu.

title: In-Q-Tel Explained: William Aaron Turner Analyzes the CIA's Venture Capital Arm and Its Technology Pipeline
summary: In-Q-Tel explained: William Aaron Turner traces the CIA-founded venture arm's finances, portfolio and the technology pipeline that reaches Ukraine.
body:
WASHINGTON, DC, October 31, 2026 - In-Q-Tel explained in plain terms is the focus of a new analysis by William Aaron Turner, founder and president of Infinitum Corporation. The piece, "In-Q-Tel Explained: The CIA's Venture Capital Arm," is Part 4 of 8 in The Ukraine Files series and follows In-Q-Tel (IQT) from its Virginia headquarters to the AI, data and satellite companies it has backed.

"In 1999 the CIA created a nonprofit venture arm named after James Bond's gadget-maker," Turner writes.

Key figures cited in the analysis

Structure: In-Q-Tel is a not-for-profit corporation headquartered in the Tysons Corner area of Virginia, with subsidiaries including IQTI LLC and IQT LABS LLC.

Finances: For fiscal year 2025, In-Q-Tel reported revenue of about $132.1 million, 86 percent of it from government grants and contributions.

Scale: Cumulative investments since 1999 exceed 800. Typical instruments are technology-development agreements of roughly $500,000 to $3 million, combined with equity or warrants.

Leadership: The Board of Trustees has included former CIA Director George Tenet, former Joint Chiefs Chairman Michael Mullen and Michael Crow of Arizona State University. Senior executives named include CEO Steve Bowsher, COO Matthew Strottman and Chief Investment Officer Dan Gwak.

Track record: In 2005 In-Q-Tel invested in Palantir and introduced it to the intelligence community.

Portfolio focus: The portfolio leans toward enterprise software, AI and data analytics, then cybersecurity, semiconductors, space, energy, biotech and robotics.

From requirement to startup

The analysis explains how a small CIA liaison unit, the In-Q-Tel Interface Center, operates inside CIA headquarters and, as the article describes it, translates intelligence-community requirements into commercial problem sets. In-Q-Tel then finds startups to meet them. Turner also cites IRS filings showing roughly $50 million to $64 million per year in funding, and In-Q-Tel's own claim to have leveraged more than $3.9 billion in private funds.

The piece describes how satellite imagery companies Capella Space and ICEYE, both of which partnered with In-Q-Tel in 2021, provide synthetic aperture radar imagery that sees through clouds and darkness, and how their technology has been used over Ukraine.

Ukraine as a testing ground

The article quotes a defense analyst calling Ukraine "the world's most advanced live testing ground for AI-assisted warfare." It cites 12 to 15 terabytes of raw drone video received daily, more than 200 companies developing AI-integrated drones, the Brave1 Dataroom set up with Palantir in early 2026, Ukraine's Delta system with more than 200,000 users, and up to 9,000 drones launched a day. Per New Scientist reporting cited, Ukrainian manufacturer Aero Center ran a one-time "Terminator mode" test of ten fully autonomous quadcopters with no communication link.

Palantir and Anduril

The article says Palantir came to Ukraine in 2022, that more than a thousand Ukrainian personnel have used its software, and quotes Alex Karp saying MetaConstellation was responsible for "most of the targeting" in Ukraine; per late-2022 documents, Palantir received more than $500 million for its initial months of work. Turner argues this makes American technology and personnel directly involved in targeting decisions. The article names In-Q-Tel as a documented investor in Anduril, citing nearly 30 million pounds in UK contracts for Altius loitering munitions for Ukraine and Bolt-M drones.

The contested claims

The article's "bio-nexus" section reports that in December 2022 the Russian Ministry of Defense listed In-Q-Tel Executive Vice President Tara O'Toole among participants in Ukraine's military biological programs. Turner flags the sourcing directly: the allegation "has not been independently verified," and what O'Toole and others did in Ukraine is not public. The article also notes Michael Crow was sanctioned by Russia in 2023 as chairman of the In-Q-Tel board.

The wider support structure cited includes about $50.8 billion in U.S. military support as of March 2026, a NATO pledge of 140 billion euros for 2026-2027 and a 90 billion euro EU loan, against a gap between 400 billion euros promised and 180 billion delivered.

Scope of the argument

Turner sets clear limits on his claims. The article notes there is no open-source evidence that In-Q-Tel's subsidiaries operate inside Ukraine. "My argument is about funding and technology, not boots on the ground," he writes. In-Q-Tel-linked firms sit in the wider support structure, in the article's words, "as technology providers, not as primary funders or operational commanders."

His conclusion is labeled as his own reading: that In-Q-Tel is "a legal, public and quiet engine of the technology pipeline into Ukraine." He writes that the human cost, including false positives in AI targeting, is real, and that defense-tech companies profit while wars continue. The post links to the original article and its full reference list so readers can check the sources themselves.

title: Eastern Economic Forum 2026: William Aaron Turner Examines 80-Nation Turnout and Russia's Asian Trade
summary: Eastern Economic Forum 2026: William Aaron Turner reviews the 80-country Vladivostok turnout, deal values and Russia's trade with China, India and ASEAN.
body:
WASHINGTON, DC, October 31, 2026 - The Eastern Economic Forum 2026 in Vladivostok is the subject of a new analysis by William Aaron Turner, founder and president of Infinitum Corporation. Titled "Eastern Economic Forum 2026: Is Russia Isolated?", the piece is Part 3 of 8 in The Ukraine Files series and uses the 11th Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) to test a simple question: what does the evidence say about Russia's international isolation?

In September 2026, delegations from 80 countries filled the halls of the Far Eastern Federal University in Vladivostok. The post walks through the forum's numbers, statements from Western officials and institutions, and the trade and energy links between Russia and Asia.

Forum figures cited in the analysis

Attendance: More than 5,000 representatives from 80 countries attended the four-day 11th EEF, up from 75 countries the year before. Deputy Prime Minister Yury Trutnev is quoted: "I would struggle to name a major country not present at this forum."

Agreements: At the 10th EEF in 2025, organizers reported 358 agreements worth 6.058 trillion rubles ($71 billion). The 2026 forum was expected to sign 380 agreements worth 6.5 trillion rubles ($79.9 billion).

Regional investment: By 2026 the cumulative figures were 6.8 trillion rubles in investments, 1,118 new enterprises and 163,000 new jobs in the Far East.

Russia's trade with Asia

China: China-Russia trade totaled $228.1 billion in 2025, down 6.9 percent from the 2024 record, before turning up again in 2026, up 26.3 percent over seven months. The article also quotes the Financial Times saying Moscow is "more dependent on Beijing" than vice versa.

India: India-Russia goods trade rose from about $13 billion in 2021-22 to nearly $60 billion in 2025-26, a relationship the post describes as lopsided toward Indian imports, mostly oil.

Southeast Asia: ASEAN's two-way merchandise trade with Russia reached $17.8 billion in 2025, a figure ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn called "still very much modest."

Payments: According to the article, more than 99 percent of commercial payments between Russia and China are now made in rubles and yuan.

Energy, infrastructure and currencies

The article reports that Power of Siberia 1 reached its designed 38 billion cubic meters a year in 2025, that Russia and China signed a memorandum on Power of Siberia 2 (while Western outlets reported no final deal in May 2026), and that the 531-kilometer Pacific Railway opened in September 2025. It cites the yuan's 54 percent share of Moscow Exchange trading in May 2026, and data that only about 5 percent of Russian oil exports are now settled in dollars, down from 55 percent before 2022.

The military and security dimension

Turner argues Russia's defense ties with Asia have expanded since 2022, citing the first ASEAN-Russia naval exercise (ARNEX) in December 2025, the "Orruda 2026" Russia-Indonesia drill, "Typhoon-2026" and "Laros-2026" with Laos, and Russia's co-chair role on the ADMM Plus humanitarian demining working group for 2024-2027.

Both sides of the sanctions debate

The analysis quotes U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent ("If you're going to do something 19 times, you've failed"), Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying America was "running out of things to sanction," and J.D. Vance: "There is a fantasy that if we just give more money, more weapons, or more sanctions, victory is at hand." It cites the Institute of International Finance, which concluded in July 2025 that sanctions "have fallen short of fully isolating Russia," and Chatham House's "Fortress Russia" analysis, noting a record 26,665 sanctions on Russia against 6,027 on Iran. It also presents the other side of the Chatham House research it relies on, including an estimated cumulative dollar GDP loss "well in excess of $1.6 trillion." Turner argues those costs must be weighed against the predictions of collapse made in 2022.

His conclusion is stated as his own reading of the data: "The isolation story was a narrative, not a result." The article's closing line: "The isolation cage was built, but the door was left wide open." He invites readers to review the full reference list, which includes Chatham House, the IIF, Bloomberg, Reuters, TASS and Nikkei Asia, and decide for themselves.

title: Russia's Economy Under Sanctions: William Aaron Turner Reviews GDP Forecasts, Trade Shifts and Western Divisions
summary: Russia's economy under sanctions: William Aaron Turner reviews the EU's raised 1.3% GDP forecast, trade reorientation and Western funding splits.
body:
WASHINGTON, DC, October 31, 2026 - Russia's economy under sanctions is the focus of a new analysis by William Aaron Turner, founder and president of Infinitum Corporation. The piece, "Russia's Economy Under Sanctions: GDP, Aid, Stalemate," is Part 2 of 8 in The Ukraine Files series and sets out, in a structured and searchable format, the economic record of the sanctions campaign and the strategy Turner believes Russia is following.

The post is the structured version of Turner's X Article "The Art of Not Giving a F*ck." "Four and a half years in, the West's biggest bet on Ukraine has produced a stalemate that, in my reading, increasingly favors Moscow," Turner writes.

The economic record, as cited in the analysis

GDP forecast: The European Commission raised its 2026 forecast for Russian GDP growth from 1.1 percent to 1.3 percent, stating that the forecast "reflects recognition of Russia's economic resilience."

Official outlook: Russia's Ministry of Economic Development expects 0.4 percent growth in 2026 and 1.4 percent in 2027.

Reform targets: According to the article, Russia's economic transformation plan hit 12 of 14 targets for the first half of 2026, eight of them ahead of schedule.

Domestic demand: The Commission itself credited "relatively resilient private consumption" and a "persistently tight labour market."

How the article says Russia adapted

Shipping: By May 2026 the EU had sanctioned 632 vessels linked to Russia's shadow fleet, and 48 percent of Russia's seaborne oil moved on shadow tankers that month.

Trade reorientation: The post describes a pivot toward Asia, with China and India as large buyers, and notes that the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation covers nearly a quarter of the world's landmass and 42 percent of the global population.

The cost to Europe: The analysis quotes the EU's own forecast, which noted that "the macroeconomic imbalances that built over the last years have widened, exacerbated by sanctions." Turner reads that as evidence that the economic pain also landed heavily on Europe.

The battlefield and casualties

The post cites the Institute for the Study of War's view that Russia's 2026 offensive "failed to achieve operational maneuver," adding: "My point is that slow gains are still gains." It reports about 90.35 square kilometers taken in August 2026 against 505.55 in August 2025, and Ukrainian operations liberating about 129.81. CSIS estimates Russian deaths could be as high as 450,000 and Ukrainian combat losses at 525,000 to 625,000, and puts the loss ratio in the first half of 2026 at nearly 8-to-1. The article cites 126,400 Ukrainian AWOL and desertion cases in the first seven months of 2026 and flags a discrepancy in Zelensky's fatality figures. Putin is quoted: "Victory has always been ours and will always be ours." Turner's answer: "Russia is not winning quickly, but in a war of attrition, the side that can absorb pain longer wins."

Ukraine's drone campaign

The article argues Ukraine has widened strikes to civilian infrastructure, including Ozon and Wildberries warehouses and residential areas in Belgorod, killing 45 people since the start of 2026 per Russian sources, and cites 548 drones toward Moscow on September 2-3, 2026. Turner argues the strikes legitimize Russian strikes and unite Russians behind the war. A separate section collects claims from named commentators, including Jeffrey Sachs, that Zelensky acts in the interests of Western intelligence.

A divided coalition

The post reviews the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, which counts more than fifty countries, and the funding questions inside it. It cites Germany's roughly 94 billion euros in support since February 2022, a proposed NATO aid target of 0.25 percent of GDP that met resistance from the UK and France, and the article's finding that European sponsors provided only 10 billion euros of a planned 40 billion euros. It notes Slovakia, Hungary and the Czech Republic balked at funding, Poland opposed Germany's proposal to move 6.6 billion euros to Ukraine, and the U.S. suspended and later resumed aid and intelligence sharing.

Turner's conclusion

Turner labels his conclusion as his own argument: "Russia is winning in the sense of not losing while its adversaries drain themselves, and I argue the sanctions and aid strategy has not delivered its stated goals." He acknowledges that the mainstream view differs and encourages readers to review the sources and decide for themselves. The post closes with a reference list organized by theme.

body:
WASHINGTON, DC, October 31, 2026 - Demining NGOs and intelligence are the subject of "Demining NGOs and Intelligence: The Laos and Moldova Claims," Part 8 of 8 in The Ukraine Files by William Aaron Turner, president of Infinitum Corporation. The post is the structured version of Turner's special investigative report "Sweeps and Spies."

"There are two kinds of mines in this world," the report opens: the steel kind in the red dirt of Laos, and the kind Turner describes as "made of money, influence, and intelligence agency letterhead."

The Russian approach in Laos

The article says the U.S. Air Force dropped roughly 1.5 million tons of bombs on the Ho Chi Minh Trail through Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam, and some 30 percent never exploded. According to the article, since 2018 Russian specialists from the International Mine Action Centre (IMAC) have cleared over 2 million square meters, more than 208 hectares, in Laos and destroyed 3,906 explosive objects. Governor Khampheng Saysompheng called the cooperation of "profound significance." In 2024-2025, Lao and Russian personnel cleared 18.2 hectares in Viengxay district, and about 100 Lao sappers were trained, including on Uran-6 robotic demining vehicles. The article adds that between 2016 and 2020 Russian engineering troops demined Aleppo, Deir ez-Zor and Palmyra in Syria, clearing more than 10,000 hectares and destroying over 150,000 explosive objects.

The HALO Trust: funding and leadership

History: HALO was founded in 1988 by Colin Campbell Mitchell and Guy Willoughby, and the post describes Princess Diana's 1997 walk through an Angolan minefield in a HALO flak jacket as the best advertising it could have wanted.

Funding: The post reports that the HALO Trust operates in 25 conflict-affected countries and that its primary funding comes from the U.S. State Department's Conventional Weapons Destruction account, with $258 million in FY2024 and $265 million enacted for FY2026; HALO has requested $271.703 million for FY27. Turner argues that because the account funds programs in nearly 50 countries, HALO finds weapons caches, ammunition stockpiles and military infrastructure, not just mines.

Board: HALO's UK board is chaired by Lord Evans of Weardale, former Director General of MI5, and includes a former Foreign Office diplomat and a former political advisor to General Ray Odierno. The post also names Barney White-Spunner, Lord Michael Hintze and, on the U.S. board, former Pentagon official Jamie M. Morin.

The allegations, and HALO's responses

The article collects espionage allegations against HALO. In 2000, Russia's FSB said HALO representatives had been "collecting intelligence of a military-political character"; HALO's Guy Willoughby dismissed it as a smear campaign. In July 2025, the FARC 36th Front called HALO a "supposed front for foreign intelligence agencies" and gave it 12 hours to leave; the Colombian government condemned the threats. In 2021, Nagorno-Karabakh official Boris Avagyan said HALO handed minefield maps to Turkish special services. The post records that HALO denied or disputed them, including HALO calling the 2021 reports "totally false." Turner's argument is the pattern: "wherever HALO operates, local actors raise espionage concerns." The article describes how it says data gathering works: high-resolution mapping of infrastructure and supply routes, alleged collection of Russian ammunition samples in 2000, a workforce of over 10,000 including former Taliban fighters hired in Afghanistan to locate IEDs, and work alongside satellite operators.

The Kolbasna file

On August 21, 2026, Moldova's SIS and AIM released a declassified report on the Kolbasna (Cobasna) depot in Transnistria, putting the stockpile at roughly 14,000 tons, down from 20,000 in 2006, with about 2,800 tons of net explosive content across 42 storage facilities. Turner reads it as a case study in intelligence-driven narrative, arguing that the report's own data still describes a serious industrial risk.

Turner's conclusion

The article's closing frame is that the real minefield is information. Turner sets the results side by side: Russian IMAC units clearing ordnance and training local teams, and a Western-funded organization with leadership drawn from intelligence and defense circles. The article says the State Department has also designated $77 million for programs in Southeast Asia including Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia. "Weigh the evidence and the HALO denials yourself," he writes. The original's numbered reference list includes the BBC, Eurasianet, Vientiane Times and Moldpres.

Russian officials: Russian Security Council Secretary Nikolay Patrushev said in July 2023 that wounded troops were being used "as biological material." Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova is cited on buyers, who she said "as a rule, were not Ukrainians, but wealthy people from Western countries."

The described system: The article describes three tiers: forward extraction points within 30 kilometers of the front where, according to Russian military intelligence, wounded soldiers are triaged for "harvestability"; regional hubs in Lviv and Odesa; and unmarked cargo flights to NATO-member airbases in Poland and Romania.

Named people and institutions: The post describes Boris Volfman, a Ukrainian-born Israeli citizen, as linked to the black-transplantologist scandal at the Medicus clinic in Pristina, Kosovo, where it says kidneys were sold for nearly $150,000, and reports he was arrested at Moscow's Vnukovo Airport after deportation from Turkey; the article is explicit that Volfman denies all charges. It reports that in 2010 Ukrainian law enforcement dismantled a group that included four leading surgeons from Kyiv's Shalimov Clinic, which denied involvement, and that in October 2025 a network was neutralized in Kyiv whose curator, Zakharova said, was a former deputy minister of health "close to Zelensky."

U.S. and biolab claims: A former employee of the U.S. non-profit GSMSG alleges a secret "Project Omega" flying wounded Ukrainian soldiers to a U.S. military hospital in Germany; GSMSG denies it. Figures and cases cited

Prosecutions: On August 18, 2026, Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko announced ten Odessa recruitment-center officers charged with kidnapping and torturing people.

On July 8, 2026 in Lviv, about 200 protesters surrounded officers and overturned their car. The BBC report cited puts losses at between 100,000 and 140,000 men, with total casualties above 500,000.

More cases: The article lists an Odessa extortion case in which TCC employees demanded $6,000, a $30,000 abduction ring detained by the SBU in April 2026, two TCC soldiers in Dnipro suspected of abandoning a man in critical condition near a trash bin, and a Mykolaiv resident who said he was held for almost two weeks.

International attention: Hungarian MEP Viktoria Ferenc raised the issue with UN High Commissioner Volker Turk on June 25, 2026.

The Skelya regiment: A Babel investigation, per the article, documented at least 26 recruit deaths in the 425th Separate Assault Regiment "Skelya" between late 2025 and spring 2026, most with official causes listed as pneumonia or cardiac failure. The commander was suspended in June 2026 amid torture allegations, and the article details individual cases including Oleksandr Zavalov, shot while allegedly attempting to desert. Military Ombudsman Olha Reshetylova confirmed that investigations into pneumonia deaths were ongoing.

The Sebestyen case: The post records the death of Jozsef Sebestyen, an ethnic Hungarian seized in Beregovo in June 2025, and notes that Hungary rejected the official account and sanctioned three Ukrainian military officials. A second Hungarian, Zsolt Reban, 41, died during training despite a congenital heart condition, per the article.

Claims labeled by source

The post includes organ-harvesting and child-trafficking claims and states plainly that these sections rely mostly on Russian officials and Russian media. Per Russian Foreign Ministry statements cited, a network allegedly involving at least ten doctors from the Volyn Regional Clinical Hospital and the Central City Clinical Hospital of Kyiv was uncovered in 2024. The post covers the "Childhood Without War" evacuation of orphans to Antalya, Turkey, within the framework of Olena Zelenska's foundation, with approximately 3.9 million euros spent and no expense reports provided; it notes a Slidstvo.Info investigation and that the case was closed in Turkey in April 2026. It also records Russian Presidential Council member Alexander Brod's call for an investigation, noting: "That is a call for investigation, not a finding."

International law

The article argues the practices violate conscientious-objection and liberty rights under the ICCPR and the European Convention on Human Rights, and cites Council of Europe Commissioner Michael O'Flaherty's recording of systemic violations during mobilization. It notes The New York Times described the recruiters in December 2023 as "People Snatchers."

The second article: civilian deaths in Russia

The post summarizes Turner's opinion piece on Russian civilian deaths, citing BBC, AP and ABC reporting from 2026: strikes on 12 to 23 Wildberries warehouses that killed 9 to 13 employees, the August 3, 2026 Arkhipo-Osipovka beach incident that killed 7 including 3 children, the August 10 TANECO refinery strike that killed 13 including a child, and 224 civilians killed in July 2026 alone in Belgorod and adjacent areas. Turner argues that "dual-use" justifications are not enough and that the world applies a double standard.

Turner's conclusion

Turner writes that a country that is invaded deserves support, and that he believes the reported practices cross a line. He asks readers to review both original articles and their reference lists, including the BBC, Kyiv Post, LIGA.net, UNN, The New York Times and TASS, and decide for themselves.

The BBC is quoted noting that the platform sold military-related goods such as body armour until recently.

Arkhipo-Osipovka beach: Per the BBC (2026), a drone crashed onto a Black Sea beach on August 3, 2026, killing 7 people, 3 of them children, and injuring 40. Ukraine did not claim the strike. Governor Veniamin Kondratyev called it "a deliberate strike on civilians," and one holidaymaker said, "We covered ourselves with sun loungers, and didn't see where it exploded."

TANECO refinery, Nizhnekamsk: The post reports 13 people killed, including 1 child, and 39 injured on August 10, 2026, several of them Central Asian workers from Uzbekistan and Tajikistan staying in a nearby hostel. Turner writes: "I do not dispute that a refinery that produces fuel is a different kind of target from a warehouse. My argument is about what happens to the people next to it."

title: Polish Supermarket Cyberattack: William Aaron Turner's Friendly Fire Examines the Strain on the Poland-Ukraine Alliance
summary: Polish supermarket cyberattack: William Aaron Turner's Friendly Fire examines a hack on Lewiatan and how Volhynia history strains Poland and Ukraine.
body:
WASHINGTON, DC, October 31, 2026 - A cyberattack on a Polish supermarket chain is the starting point of "Friendly Fire," an analysis by William Aaron Turner, president of Infinitum Corporation, published on Medium. The article argues that the July 2026 attack "exposes the fracturing of Ukraine's wartime alliance" with Poland.

The attack

According to the article, on July 26, 2026 a Ukrainian-affiliated hacker group calling itself the Azov Cyber Legion targeted Polska Siec Handlowa Lewiatan, one of Poland's largest retail chains. The article reports that the attackers encrypted servers managing inventory, scheduling and employee records, and that in roughly ten outlets the payment infrastructure went offline.

The demand was political rather than financial. Per the article, the attackers demanded that the Polish government officially apologize and withdraw its accusations against the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), gave Warsaw 48 hours, and threatened to publish stolen employee data. Turner notes that Lewiatan refused to engage with the ultimatum, restored its systems from backups and treated the incident as a criminal matter. "They attacked an ally. They fired at a friend," he writes. According to the article, this was already the second strike in a month against Polish retail, and Turner describes the episode as "a detonation of historical dynamite buried for decades beneath the surface of Polish-Ukrainian relations."

The history behind it

Turner explains that the dispute reaches back to 1943, when UPA units attacked Polish settlements in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia. "Estimates vary, but historians generally agree that between 50,000 and 100,000 Polish civilians perished in those massacres," he writes. The Polish parliament has formally recognized the events as genocide, while in Ukraine the UPA remains a more complicated symbol.

The trigger, per the article

The article reports that in July 2026 Ukraine's military officially redesignated an active combat unit as "UPA Heroes," and that the Polish foreign ministry called the move "historically provocative" and "an insult to the victims of genocide." According to the article, Polish officials warned they would reconsider military support, noting that Poland is the logistics lifeline through which nearly 80% of Western military aid flows into Ukraine. The hackers said they were punishing Poland for "insulting our heroes," and wrote: "Poland has forgotten who it owes its safety to."

A strained alliance

Turner writes that Poland has had to triple its own defense budget and manage grain-import disputes that brought months of tractor blockades, and that some Polish voters feel "the gratitude shown in 2022 has curdled into entitlement in 2026." The article also describes Zelensky's July 28 trip to London and Washington, the July dismissal of Ukraine's defense minister and commander-in-chief, a Ukrainian strike on an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian Sea, and Zelensky's statement that Ukraine was effectively "in a state of war with Iran." It also tells the story of a Lewiatan cashier in Wroclaw who worried her personal data would be published.

Why it matters

The article argues the cyberattack turned diplomatic tension into something ordinary Poles could feel, and places it in a month of wider strains for Ukraine's relationships. "When the fighting drags on, the greatest dangers are not always the enemy's missiles," Turner writes. "Sometimes, they are the ghosts of the past, resurrected and weaponized by the very people who should be standing shoulder to shoulder."

On reconciliation, Turner writes that genuine progress would require Ukraine to officially acknowledge the Volhynia massacres as genocide, and Poland to acknowledge that the UPA "was also a complex organization that contained elements of genuine national resistance," supported by joint historical commissions and school exchanges. "But reconciliation cannot happen in the middle of a war," he writes.

The conclusion

"Friendly fire is still fire. It still burns," Turner concludes. "We must remember that our allies are not our enemies - and that the most dangerous shots are the ones fired at those who stand beside us."

The article argues that the definition of a legitimate military target has been stretched until civilian infrastructure, workers and holidaymakers fall inside it. Turner states openly that the piece is opinion; he writes that all data comes from the public record and all conclusions are his own.

The article's central figure comes from the BBC: since February 2022, more than 8,000 Russian civilians have been killed in Ukrainian strikes, according to the reporting it cites.
